title: Phonetics
html:
Phonetics carries about 2 of the 16 English questions (our estimate), and the official model paper shows exactly what they look like: "The word 'procrastination' has its stress on the … syllable" and "Which of the following pairs have the same initial vowel sound? (ago, alone)". Both are answerable with a short rule set and a little practice reading phonetic values aloud.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • The 44 phonemes of Received Pronunciation: 20 vowels (12 pure + 8 diphthongs) and 24 consonants.
  • Same-sound and different-sound word pairs (initial vowel, final consonant, silent letters).
  • Number of syllables and the syllable that carries the primary stress.
  • Stress shift between noun and verb, and sentence stress on content words.

3.2 Phonemes (vowels and consonants)

English spelling is not phonetic, so we count sounds, not letters. A phoneme is the smallest unit of sound that changes meaning (ship /ʃɪp/ versus sheep /ʃiːp/ — the pair is a minimal pair).

Vowels (20). Twelve monophthongs (single, steady sounds): short /ɪ e æ ʌ ɒ ʊ ə/ and long /iː ɑː ɔː uː ɜː/. Eight diphthongs (glides): /eɪ aɪ ɔɪ aʊ əʊ ɪə eə ʊə/. Examples:

Sound Words Sound Words
/iː/ seat, feel, key /ɪ/ sit, inn, village
/e/ bed, head, said /æ/ cat, apple
/ɑː/ car, father, calm /ʌ/ cup, up, love
/ɒ/ hot, on, watch /ɔː/ all, caught, door, more
/ʊ/ put, foot, good /uː/ food, blue, rule
/ɜː/ bird, learn, her /ə/ ago, alone, sofa (schwa)
/eɪ/ day, break, eight /aɪ/ my, high, buy
/ɔɪ/ boy, coin /aʊ/ now, owl, house
/əʊ/ go, home, boat /ɪə/ here, ear, beer

The schwa /ə/ is the commonest vowel sound in English and occurs only in unstressed syllables: ago /əˈgəʊ/ and alone /əˈləʊn/ begin with the same sound, while owl /aʊl/ and all /ɔːl/, inn /ɪn/ and eel /iːl/, up /ʌp/ and on /ɒn/ do not. Vowel length matters: bit /ɪ/ versus beat /iː/; pull /ʊ/ versus pool /uː/.

Consonants (24). Plosives /p b t d k g/; fricatives /f v θ ð s z ʃ ʒ h/; affricates /tʃ dʒ/; nasals /m n ŋ/; liquids /l r/; glides /j w/. Voiceless versus voiced pairs: /p b/, /t d/, /k g/, /f v/, /θ ð/, /s z/, /ʃ ʒ/, /tʃ dʒ/. - /θ/ (voiceless) in thin, think, bath; /ð/ (voiced) in this, then, bathe. - /ʃ/ in ship, nation, sure; /ʒ/ in vision, measure, pleasure; /tʃ/ in chair, ture; /dʒ/ in jug, general, badge. - /ŋ/ in sing, think; /h/ in hat; /j/ in yes, use. - Silent letters: k in knife, know; b in climb, comb, doubt, debt; w in write, answer; p in psychology, pneumonia; g in gnat, sign; h in hour, honest; l in walk, calm; t in listen, castle; n in autumn, column. - The same letter can give different sounds: c in cat /k/ and city /s/; s in sun /s/ and rose /z/; -ed is /t/ after voiceless sounds (walked), /d/ after voiced (played), /ɪd/ after /t d/ (wanted); -s is /s/, /z/ or /ɪz/ (cats, dogs, buses).

3.3 Syllables and stress (word and sentence)

A syllable has one vowel sound: beau-ti-ful (3), ed-u-ca-tion (4), com-mu-ni-ca-tion (5), pro-cras-ti-na-tion (5). Count vowel sounds: the-ater is 3, name is 1.

Word stress is the syllable pronounced louder, longer and higher. Rules of thumb: - Words ending -tion, -sion, -ic, -ical, -ity, -ify, -ian, -ious stress the syllable before the ending: edu-CA-tion, pro-cras-ti-NA-tion, eco-NOM-ic, ca-PA-ci-ty, pho-TOG-ra-pher. - Words ending -graphy, -logy, -ate, -ment (long words): pho-TOG-ra-phy, bi-OL-o-gy, ECO-no-my → e-CON-o-my. - Two-syllable nouns and adjectives are usually stressed on the first syllable (TAble, PREsent, REcord); two-syllable verbs on the second (preSENT, reCORD, deCIDE). Stress shift marks the change of word class: a PREsent / to preSENT; an INcrease / to inCREASE; a REcord / to reCORD; an OBject / to obJECT. - Compound nouns are stressed on the first part (BLACKboard, GREENhouse); compound adjectives and verbs on the second (bad-TEMpered, underSTAND). - Prefixes are generally unstressed (re-TURN, un-HAPpy); suffixes -ful, -less, -ness, -ing do not move the stress (BEAUtiful).

Sentence stress. In connected speech, content words (nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs, negatives, question words) carry the stress; function words (articles, prepositions, auxiliaries, pronouns, conjunctions) are weak and their vowels reduce to /ə/. I want to go to the market. Stress changes the focus: I didn't steal the money (I did something else) versus I didn't steal the money (another money). Intonation: a falling tune for statements, wh-questions and commands; a rising tune for yes/no questions and uncertain lists (the last item of a list falls).

Phonetics traps

Count sounds, not letters (knife starts with /n/, hour with a vowel, so an hour). -ed has three sounds. Pairs that look alike do not sound alike: cough, though, through, tough, thought. The stress of a long word follows its ending, not its beginning.

Formula and fact sheet

Item Fact
RP phonemes 20 vowels (12 + 8) + 24 consonants = 44
schwa /ə/, unstressed only
-tion words stress on the syllable before
noun / verb pair PREsent / preSENT
sentence stress content words, not function words
/θ/ vs /ð/ thin vs this

Chapter summary

  • English has 44 phonemes in RP; a silent letter adds no sound.
  • Words ending in -tion, -ic, -ity stress the preceding syllable.
  • Two-syllable nouns take first-syllable stress, verbs second.
  • Weak function words reduce to schwa; content words carry sentence stress.

Practice questions

Set A — Recall (12 questions)

  1. The number of vowel phonemes (including diphthongs) in Received Pronunciation isa5b12c20d24
  2. The number of consonant phonemes in English isa21b24c26d20
  3. The number of syllables in "beautiful" isa3b4c2d5
  4. The word "procrastination" has its primary stress on the ___ syllable.a2ndb3rdc5thd4th
  5. Which pair has the same initial vowel sound?aup, onbago, alonecinn, eeldowl, all
  6. Which word contains the voiceless /θ/ sound?athinbthiscthendbathe
  7. Which word contains the /ʃ/ sound?achairbmeasurecjudgedship
  8. In which word is the letter "b" silent?abubblebrubbercclimbdbring
  9. Which word contains a diphthong?abitbbedccutdboy
  10. The noun "present" is stressed on theasecond syllablebfirst syllableceither syllabledneither syllable
  11. In a sentence, stress usually falls onacontent wordsbarticlescprepositionsdauxiliaries
  12. Which word has the long vowel /uː/?aputbfootcfooddgood
Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (c) — 12 monophthongs + 8 diphthongs.

2. (b) — 24 consonant phonemes.

3. (a) — beau-ti-ful.

4. (d) — pro-cras-ti-NA-tion; stress falls before -tion.

5. (b) — both begin with the schwa /ə/.

6. (a) — thin has /θ/; this, then, bathe have /ð/.

7. (d) — ship /ʃ/; measure has /ʒ/; chair /tʃ/; judge /dʒ/.

8. (c) — climb /klaɪm/.

9. (d) — boy /ɔɪ/.

10. (b) — noun: PREsent; verb: preSENT.

11. (a) — content words carry the stress.

12. (c) — food /fuːd/; put, foot, good have /ʊ/.

Set B — Understanding (6 questions)

  1. In "photographer" the primary stress is on thea1st syllableb2nd syllablec3rd syllabled4th syllable
  2. The number of syllables in "communication" isa4b6c5d3
  3. Which word contains the /ʒ/ sound?avisionbviciouscvisitdvivid
  4. The words "ship" and "sheep" differ inaa consonantba vowelcstressdnumber of syllables
  5. In "psychology" the silent letter isaybscldp
  6. The word "economy" has primary stress on thea1st syllableb3rd syllablec2nd syllabled4th syllable
Answers and explanations — Set B

1. (b) — pho-TOG-ra-pher: the stress is on the second syllable, as in pho-TOG-ra-phy.

2. (c) — com-mu-ni-ca-tion.

3. (a) — vision /ˈvɪʒn/; vicious has /ʃ/.

4. (b) — /ɪ/ versus /iː/: a minimal pair.

5. (d) — the initial p is not pronounced: /saɪˈkɒlədʒi/.

6. (c) — e-CON-o-my.
